Author

  • Open Relationshipderu

    First part completed: July 2024

    Download PDF

A documentary queer drama about finding oneself in a space where the boundaries of love are blurred and honesty is the hardest challenge. Through candid monologues and descriptions of everyday reality, the text explores the complexities of breaking away from conventional roles and monogamous expectations, turning intimate experiences into political and personal drama.

Staged reading, Reforum Space Budva, Montenegro (February 2025)

Staged reading, Munich (October 2025, directed by: Alexander Löwen, translation: David Drevs)

Staged reading, Echo Lubimovka, Los Angeles (November 2026, directed by: Dima Barch, translation: Rostislav Godlevsky)

1.

I think the corniest cliché for an opening scene is:

Morning. A clock. The kind of alarm clock with big red digits. The time is 8:59 a.m. A nasty synthetic beep-beep-beep-beep goes off, and the hero's hand, with deliberate clumsiness, tries to reach it, knocking over some stuff and the alarm clock itself.

In this scene the alarm is switched off with one precise movement.

This is how the author wants to show that the hero has precisely planned his morning and everything's generally under his control. Or at least that's what he thinks.

The word "hero" pisses me off, and spinning out this pretentious discourse about deconstructing the traditional hero, the search for an everyday hero, the antihero, the meta-hero and blah-blah-blah is the last fucking thing anybody needs, so the word "hero" is now going to appear in this text for the last time.

The hero turns off the alarm.

He is lying on an IKEA couch on a gray IKEA sheet. The fitted kind, with elastic on all four sides. In the evening, when he was pulling two of its corners over the couch and trying to get the third one on, the first two kept popping off, and he had to start all over again. Sometimes this battle goes on for a very long time.

His name is Igor. He is 36 years old. He is lying on a couch in a flat at

81673, Weihenstephaner Straße 10, Munich.

Why so many details?

This is supposed to be a documentary play. My name really is Igor. I turn off the alarm on my phone and see that my boyfriend is heading out somewhere at 9 a.m. In answer to my question "Where are you going?" he says he's arranged a quickie.

Rostislav. I won't be long. You don't mind?

I say I don't, even though I barely understand what's going on, whether I'm even awake, and, most importantly, whether I really don't mind.

We've been together for three years, and for the last six months we've been in an open relationship.

Igor. The sound of the front door closing. Pause. Igor lies on the gray sheet and stares at the ceiling.

Open Relationship

Igor Sergeev

A documentary play
Translated from the Russian by Rostislav Godlevsky

2.

Igor. I open Gr[ee]ndr. Actually, it's pronounced Gr[ai]ndr, but in Saint Petersburg I used to say it like that.

It's a dating app, people here are mostly just looking for sex.

Meanwhile, "grind" means to mince or to crush. What did they mean when they named the app that?

All profiles are just photos.

First one. a guy. 26, standing against a mountain backdrop.

Second profile. No face. 39 years old. profile with a photo of a river and the sun. "Spontaneous and horny when I'm online. I'm a top and I like outdoor activities. But not only that. Text me."

Third profile. Pumped bare torso in black and white. No face. shot from below as if you're kneeling before him.

Igor. Not bad

Fourth one. a guy in a dog mask. I like it WRAFF! barking in: English

Fifth. Cute guy with a beard and a cap standing in a chandelier museum.

Next profile. A guy staring directly into the camera. Medium close-up shot.

Head shaved clean.

Blue eyes and unruly eyebrows. You can't see it in the photo, but one of his eyes is partly brown.

In the nose, a silvery ring.

Beard. Big lips, especially the bottom one. Mouth slightly open. He often does that during sex.

Big silver rings with a ball in each ear.

In this photo he's shirtless. Broad and slightly muscular shoulders. All his life he's worried that he's too skinny, goes to the gym and really wants to be a hulking wall of muscle. But now he's lost some weight again and I love it.

I have a savior complex and I always liked guys who, through how they looked and behaved, signaled that they needed to be pulled out of the inescapable abyss like right now. I understand that it's not okay.

His nickname in the app is an emoji of two crossed swords. Actually, his name is Rostislav. My boyfriend, who just arranged a quickie.

300m away.
Now online.

Stats

● Height: 182cm
● Weight: 68kg
● Status: Open relationship

The app tracks the location in real time. Now he's already 500m away. 700m. 1km. and will soon disappear from Grindr's profile grid.

4.

Isarvorstadt is a central district of Munich, along the Isar river. It's like the Fontanka in Petersburg.

A very jittery guy, a little over forty. Photos of his husband on every side of the bedroom. Pretty much looking at us, banging each other. At the moment the husband's on tour. Turns out, he doesn't know his boyfriend can bring someone home. He didn't mention it before.

5.

Igor. Three years ago I was living in Saint-Petersburg. That's where Rost and I met. I come to the theater, my play is on today. I see our technical director interviewing some guy for the job. I've never seen him here before.

Acting like I'm just going about my business, I walk by. I walk by again. And again. Again. Once more. Feels like I'm totally getting clocked, but I can't help myself.

The interview ends and I pounce on her with questions:

- Who was that?

- Rostislav. A new tech, maybe a sound engineer.

- He's not gay, is he?

- Nah, definitely not.

After that story I probably come across as a total creep.

Rost has been working at the theater for about a month now. Another show has just ended. The crew is striking the set, my co-author and I are sitting in the office, Rost walks by us holding a projector and, for some reason, suddenly gives us a silent, mysterious smile, while we're sitting right next to each other. Leaves.

We've no idea what just happened. Which one of us was he smiling at?

We make a deal that next time he walks in we'll both smile back and that'll clear things up.

I am absolutely certain I don't stand a chance.

He walks in again, smiles again, we silently smile back. From outside it must look like some kind of nuthouse. He leaves again and my friend says that she's sure as hell lost this game.

That same evening the two of us go to "Zaliv". Sitting at the bar drinking countless nastoyka shots, I suggest we go to mine.

On our way we stop to buy some smokes, he buys camel blue and I think: "how is that possible?" They're the only ones I've smoked for the last several years.

When you're very alike, it's great.

But in some things it's better to be completely different, otherwise, at some point, handling a bunch of problems in emigration will be impossible for two people who are so alike.

6.

Schwabing. A neighborhood north of central Munich.

A student from Turkey. He was really worried that he didn't speak German well. And my English is awful. Turns out he'd lived in Tolyatti for a few years and speaks Russian.

7.

Igor. I am in the middle of this documentary playwriting course and by the end of it I have to finish this play.

After the first lecture I realize that eventually I'll have to write a piece that treats interviews, documents and diaries with great care and diligence. From all of this I, for some reason, decide that there's no room left for me in this play. That's when I start to get angry.

In addition to that, it's a massive problem for me to talk about myself. About how I'm really doing. About what I'm thinking and feeling right now. About my work, my ups and downs.

Until you ask me

Until you honestly ask me:

"how are you?"

I can just listen for hours. I tell myself: it's okay, I'm modest and I'm fighting my huge ego. But in reality I want you to ask me:
"How are you? I really want to know how you're actually doing right now?"

And then I'll pour it all out on you.

All this sounds especially great in a text where I've been talking only about myself for six pages straight.

If you keep suppressing something inside you your whole life, at some point it's gonna burst out for sure.

And then Jeffrey Dahmer, suppressing his homosexuality, will invite Steven Hicks over for a beer, hit him over the head with a dumbbell and eat his liver in a red wine and thyme sauce, with a side of fried Jerusalem artichoke.

Or, well, you'll write a play about yourself and your open relationship, treat yourself to this self-indulgent sentence about Jeffrey Dahmer, and finally tell everyone how you're actually doing.

8.

Moosach. Northwest of the city

Designer. We see each other a lot. I teach him Russian, he teaches me German. I'm crazy about his tiny apartment. It feels like time stopped there in 2005 and you're on Komenda in St. Pete's.

9.

Igor. A couple days after mobilization started, Rost said that if they came for him or grabbed him on the street, he'd slit his wrists.

But first there was February 24th. My English teacher's from Kyiv, and like three weeks before the 24th I'm telling her, totally sure of myself, that if our grandpa starts a war, it's all gonna crumble here.

Feb. 24th at 6:12am I receive a voice message from her:

"Good morning. It's started here. If possible, do something. Please, try something to make it stop."

Second or third rally.

We go around the cosmonauts, that’s what we call the riot cops, through little side streets and courtyards, and at a traffic light this old lady asks:

- What’s all the shouting about?

We say: “No to war and all that”

And she’s like: “What war?”

Rost and I figure, okay, maybe that happens, maybe she just doesn’t know. Dead serious, we tell her what’s going on. She listens really carefully, doesn’t interrupt, and then says:

“We didn’t start no war, we, actually, are ending it.”

And then, for the first time from a live human being on the street, I hear the ‘eight years’ mantra.

And even then we’re still hoping for something.

10.

Haidhausen. East of Munich.

I’m here the most. It’s close to home and looks a bit like Petersburg.

A couple. Both over forty and been together for ages. The most textbook successful gay couple, straight out of a commercial. Great sex, never saw them again.

Do you know the difference between hunger and appetite? Hunger is what our body tells us we need. Appetite is what we want.

Igor. Let's. It is a Christian world now. No place left for believers in the gods. That is why we are here, to find a new home.

12.

Fürstenried. South-west Munich. The city ends right past it.

Another couple. Waiters. They work together. Next day one of them hints at meeting up without the other, looks like his partner doesn’t know about it.

13.

September 2022.

Rost says that if they came for him or grabbed him on the street, he’d slit his wrists.

We bought tickets to Vladikavkaz, and from there it’s Upper Lars and Georgia.

Exactly 24 hours to pack. In one day we stuffed our whole life into trash bags and took it to storage. We’re in a taxi at night, going to the train station, I’m looking at the city and wondering if there’s any guarantee I’ll ever see all this again.

Back then I didn’t know for sure if I had an exit ban on me or not. Trying to figure this out through lawyers, but it’s the same hell and chaos there as everywhere else. The whole way I’m trying to convince Rost that if they don’t let me out, he goes on without me and I go back to Petersburg and we’ll sort it out later.

From Vladikavkaz to Lars we went by bike and got to the checkpoint by nightfall. And we were lucky at that, because of the bikes. The line of cars hasn’t moved for days, and the vibe in the Upper Lars chat was like:

“They say the border is closed, is it true?”

“Guys, I beg you, let my wife and three kids through, one’s a baby. Food’s out, gas is almost out.”

“Please don’t just walk past, give whatever food and drinks you’ve got” “one man helped us find food. i can share his number. he can help with lots of things”

“Guys, morning y’all, can you drink the water from those pipes sticking out of the mountain?”

“It’s a sewer”

“I think you can, it’s spring water. Our guys drank it. For sure not sewage”

“Lower Lars, don’t let the locals into the oncoming lane!!! Get out there and be a human shield!!!Don’t you get that they’re the reason you haven’t moved in a whole day? The people ahead of you have been waiting even longer, they’re about to run out of gas and then everything’s stuck for good!!”

And so it’s 3am and we’re in line on the finish stretch to passport control.

R. You could already hear from the start of the line how one of the officers was, let’s just say, doing her job more emotionally than everyone else, so I was kinda scared of her. I was just praying I wouldn’t get her, because, like, you could smell the fire coming from that little booth of hers. My turn comes, and I realize I’m going straight to her. By her voice she was this, like, imposing woman, but a real grump. I was picturing your classic government-office lady. I come up to the counter and, somewhat taken aback, see her huge long nails, this, like, absolutely luxurious kind of makeup, and in general she appeared much younger than she sounded. I hand over my passport. First she asks, like, my date of birth, and then my father’s name, which makes me stop and think a bit, because sure, I have a patronymic, but I don’t really use my father’s name in life, ‘cause he’s not in my life. So I’m like:

‘Ummm, Yuri, I think.’ And then she asks me something that makes me start wondering how real any of this is. She looks at me and asks: What’s your star sign? Aquarius, I say. She gives me back my passport and says ‘Have a good trip.’ I say thanks.

I. While we were in line, I was watching how it all worked up ahead and thinking if they let him through and not me, we’ll only get to say goodbye from a distance, through the turnstiles.

I walk up to the counter. Hand out my papers.

The border guard asks:

What’s my name? Where was I born?

Tells me to hold my head straight for the camera, and the whole time I’m answering she looks at the screen, then at me, says nothing, back at the screen, back at me, says nothing. Feels like it’s been going on forever. No idea what that was, maybe she’s got some kind of lie detector in that camera, but she sure knows how to build suspense.

Asks where else I’ve been. I start listing: Estonia, Finland, Belarus, Germany, Israel, Egypt. At some point I freeze up, but I guess that’s all she needs - she just stamps it and lets me through.

I even got through faster than Rost. But then they let him through too. And he kisses me right there past the checkpoint, in front of everyone.

14.

According to a study published in the Journal of Social and Personal Relationships in 2018, couples in open relationships don’t show a significantly higher breakup rate than monogamous couples.

15.

Haidhausen.

Classic gym jock. Really hard to tell how old he is: maybe 40, maybe 50 or even more. Decided not to ask. Very emotional and all over the place. Leaving, it turned out we go to the same gym.

16.

It was only after six months of open relationship that we realized we should probably agree on some clear rules. Each of us is allowed sex on the side, but our relationship comes first, and whatever happens out there shouldn’t turn into romantique. If romantique suddenly shows up on the horizon, we tell each other right away.

For me it’s important that we give each other a heads-up about possible sex in advance. And the main thing is that each of us can always say it’s not okay for him right now, and that it would be taken normally.

And when one of us gets back from one of these outings, he usually tells some exciting story about how it all went.

17.

Igor. One a.m.

I’m sitting alone at a bar. Scrolling Grindr. I never text anyone first. But everyone texting me right now is way off. I go outside for a smoke.

A message on Grindr:

Martin. 0 Meter entfernt. Du liest die Nachricht, während ich sie schreibe.

Igor. Fun. Wo bist du?

He’s somewhere really close. Zero meters from me, and he can see me reading his message.

I’m standing by the window, but I can’t see where he is.

Oh, there he is, a guy with a ‘stache and a cap.

In person he’s even cuter.

He’s smiling at me.

No idea how to react.

He’s with friends. I go back in, sit back down at the bar. Trying to check him out without getting clocked. He sees it.

Okay, fine. I keep drinking my beer, scrolling Grindr, if he wants to he’ll text or come over. He’s here with friends, after all.
Drinking beer

Scrolling Grindr

Drinking beer

Scrolling Grindr

Beer’s gone. He’s still with his friends, but I think he’s forgotten about me by now. Time to head home.

Someone sits down next to me. It’s him.

He asks:

“How am I doing?”

I say not great.

My German is terrible, but I tell him I have to speak it, or I’ll never learn it. I keep asking him to say everything again, he patiently explains it all.

He asks why I’m sad. Right off the bat I pour it all out on him, about me and Rost and our open relationship, and how there’s been some weird shit between us lately.

Martin switches into therapist mode. Half an hour later I feel totally calm, more so than ever. Now we’re already kissing for some reason. He’s from Berlin, came to Munich for work, says he’s sleeping at the office tonight.

I say an office is great, a real thrill ride, let’s go to your office. He plays coy, it’s awkward for him, there’s only a tiny stupid couch there. But here we are, already heading to that office. He jokingly calls me Schlampe, back then I don’t know yet what that is. But I’ll be calling him Schlampe every time we meet after that, until he says it’s actually starting to scare him. But I’m just like a kid, repeating my first swears in a foreign language.

Alyona. Basically, open relationships are cool, but I don't think it's, like, some kind of relationship of the future. I don't think that sooner or later everyone has to get there. And in general, I don't see it as a cure-all even in my own life. I'm into different formats, different periods of my life, I need something different, and I think the main thing about it is to listen really carefully to what you feel and to understand what you want at this specific moment, and on top of that it's also important to understand that at the very beginning, when you've only just met, and you're in some kind of, I don't know, flirting phase, it's totally normal not to know what you want from each other. All that only gets figured out with time, with the experience of listening to yourself and to your partner, your partner and partners. And I think it's really important here not to bullshit yourself, like "nah, I'm not jealous at all, I'm not anything, I don't give a damn who he's fucking". I mean, like, really paying attention to your own feelings. If there's something you don't like, that's a reason to at least think about it, figure it out on your own.
